questions.q: Why can't built-in tests like not_null and unique catch a case like orders.amount coming out negative?
options: Because not_null and unique don't exist in dbt
Because a negative amount is structurally valid data (not null, not a duplicate) — it's wrong by business rule, not by structure, which is exactly what a custom test is for
Because custom tests run before built-in tests and overwrite their results
Because negative numbers are not allowed in Snowflake columns
questions.explain: not_null and unique check structural properties; a business rule like "never negative" needs a custom generic test written specifically to check it.

questions.q: What should a {% test %} block's query return for a row that FAILS the check?
options: The row itself — dbt treats any row returned by a generic test's query as a test failure
An error message string
A boolean TRUE value in a dedicated column
Nothing — failing rows are never returned
questions.explain: A generic test's query selects the rows that violate the rule; any row returned counts as a failure, and zero rows returned means the test passes.

questions.q: Why does the non_negative test's definition use model and column_name as parameters rather than hardcoding orders and amount?
options: column_name is required syntax but has no actual effect
dbt requires every test to have exactly these two parameter names
So the same test definition can be reused on any column of any model via .yml, instead of writing a separate test per column
Hardcoded values run faster in Snowflake
questions.explain: Parameterizing by model and column_name is what makes a generic test reusable anywhere, applied in .yml exactly like unique or not_null.

questions.q: Once non_negative is defined under tests/generic/, how is it applied to orders.amount?
options: It applies automatically to every numeric column in the project with no configuration
By running a special dbt apply-test command
In a .yml schema file, listed under that column's tests, exactly the same way unique or not_null would be applied
By calling it directly inside orders.sql with a macro call
questions.explain: Once defined, dbt treats a custom generic test identically to a built-in one at the point of use — applied via .yml under a column's tests list.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a test is a stronger enforcement mechanism than a code comment stating the same rule?
options: A test runs automatically on every dbt build with no one needing to remember it, while a comment relies on every future developer reading and honoring it
Comments slow down query performance, unlike tests
Comments are not supported in dbt projects
Tests and comments are functionally identical
questions.explain: A test turns a business rule into an enforced, automatically-checked fact rather than a belief that depends on someone remembering to read a comment.
